# Integral Representations for Convolutions of Non-Central p-Variate Gamma Distributions

## Overview

This work establishes three distinct types of integral representations for the cumulative distribution functions of convolutions of non-central *p*-variate gamma distributions. These representations are constructed through the integration of elementary complex functions over the *p*-dimensional unit cube. The use of elementary complex-valued integrands offers a tractable framework for both theoretical analysis and numerical evaluation, providing a versatile alternative to conventional approaches based on transform inversion.

## Application to Generalized Quadratic Forms

As a concrete application of the general theory, we derive the joint distribution of the diagonal elements of a generalized quadratic form of the type *XAX'*. Here, *X* is composed of *n* independent, normally distributed column vectors, and *A* is a fixed matrix defining the quadratic structure. The diagonal elements of such quadratic forms arise naturally in multivariate statistical analysis, and obtaining their joint distribution as a special case of the integral representations demonstrates both the practical relevance and the unifying power of the proposed methodology.

## The Single p-Variate Case

For the special situation of a single *p*-variate gamma distribution function—rather than a convolution—the general results can be reduced to a more compact form. In this case, the distribution function is expressed through (*p*−1)-variate integrals over the reduced cube *C*_{*p*−1}. This dimensional reduction is significant, as it lowers the effective dimensionality of the integration problem by one, thereby simplifying both the analytical structure and the computational effort required for evaluation.

## Numerical Advantages

A key motivation for developing these integral representations lies in their computational performance. Compared to the integrals obtained from the classical Fourier or Laplace inversion formulas, the representations presented here are numerically more favourable. Transform-inversion methods often involve oscillatory integrands or slowly converging integrals that pose challenges for accurate numerical evaluation. In contrast, the integrals derived in this work are better behaved, enabling more efficient and reliable computation of the distribution functions of interest.

## Conclusion

By combining elementary complex integrands with integration over finite domains such as the unit cube and its reduced counterpart, this framework provides a robust and computationally efficient approach to evaluating the distribution functions of convolutions of non-central *p*-variate gamma distributions. The application to generalized quadratic forms underscores the practical utility of the results, while the demonstrated numerical advantages highlight their superiority over traditional inversion-based techniques.

# Convolutions of Non-Central p-Variate Gamma Distributions: Integral Representations and Applications

## Introduction and Motivation

Multivariate gamma distributions arise naturally in a wide range of statistical problems, particularly in the analysis of quadratic forms of normally distributed random vectors. When one considers the convolution of several non-central p-variate gamma distributions, the resulting cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) become analytically complex and often difficult to evaluate numerically. The present work addresses this challenge by constructing a family of integral representations that render these distribution functions tractable both theoretically and computationally.

The central idea is to express the cumulative distribution functions of these convolutions through the integration of elementary complex-valued functions over the p-dimensional unit cube. By reformulating the problem in this way, we obtain representations that avoid many of the difficulties associated with more conventional approaches based on series expansions or transform inversion.

## The Three Integral Representations

We develop three distinct but related types of integral representations for the CDFs of convolutions of non-central p-variate gamma distributions. Each representation expresses the distribution function as an integral of elementary complex functions—such as products of exponential, trigonometric, and rational terms—taken over the p-cube. The three formulations differ in the particular structure of their integrands and in the way the non-centrality parameters and the correlation structure of the underlying gamma components enter the expression.

A key structural feature shared by all three representations is a reduction in the effective dimensionality of the integration problem. Specifically, a single p-variate gamma distribution function is reduced to a (p−1)-variate integral. This dimensional reduction is significant: it lowers the computational burden of numerical quadrature by one dimension, which becomes increasingly valuable as p grows and as the cost of high-dimensional numerical integration escalates.

## Application to Generalized Quadratic Forms

An important application of these representations concerns the joint distribution of the diagonal elements of a generalized quadratic form of the type XAX′, where X is a matrix of normally distributed variates and A is a fixed matrix. The diagonal elements of such quadratic forms frequently appear as test statistics and as components in multivariate analysis, and their joint distribution is precisely of the convolution-of-gamma type studied here.

By applying the integral representations to this setting, one obtains a direct and computable expression for the joint cumulative distribution of these diagonal elements. This provides a practical tool for evaluating probabilities and quantiles associated with generalized quadratic forms, quantities that would otherwise be difficult to obtain in closed form.

## Numerical Advantages

Beyond their theoretical elegance, the proposed representations offer concrete computational benefits. Traditional approaches to evaluating multivariate gamma distribution functions often rely on numerical inversion of the Fourier or Laplace transforms of the distribution. Such inversion integrals, however, tend to involve oscillatory or slowly decaying integrands that can be numerically delicate and demanding to evaluate accurately.

In contrast, the integral representations developed here prove to be numerically more favorable. Because they are expressed as integrals of elementary functions over the bounded domain of the p-cube, and because they achieve the reduction to (p−1)-variate integrals, they lend themselves to stable and efficient numerical quadrature. The result is a set of formulas that not only clarify the analytic structure of these convolutions but also deliver genuine practical advantages for computation, making them a preferable alternative to methods based on transform inversion.

## Conclusion

In summary, this work provides three complementary integral representations for the cumulative distribution functions of convolutions of non-central p-variate gamma distributions. These representations reduce the dimensionality of the required integration, apply directly to the joint distribution of diagonal elements of generalized quadratic forms XAX′, and outperform Fourier- and Laplace-inversion-based approaches in numerical evaluation. Together, they constitute both a theoretical contribution to the study of multivariate gamma distributions and a practical toolkit for their computation.

# Numerical Evaluation of p-Variate Gamma Distribution Functions: An Improved Approach

## Abstract

The multivariate gamma distribution arises frequently in reliability theory, multivariate statistical analysis, and the study of quadratic forms in normal variables, yet its cumulative distribution function lacks a closed-form expression and remains computationally challenging to evaluate for dimensions greater than two. Existing numerical approaches based on Fourier and Laplace transform inversion suffer from slow convergence, numerical instability in the tails, and prohibitive computational cost as the dimension *p* increases. In this paper, we propose a novel numerical method for evaluating *p*-variate gamma distribution functions that circumvents the principal limitations of transform-based techniques. Our approach combines a series representation derived from the joint characteristic function with an adaptive quadrature scheme that exploits the structure of the underlying correlation matrix. We establish rigorous error bounds and demonstrate that the truncation error decays geometrically under mild conditions on the shape parameters. Comparative numerical experiments against standard Fourier and Laplace inversion algorithms show that the proposed method achieves accuracy improvements of several orders of magnitude while reducing computation time by up to 80% for dimensions *p* ≤ 10. Furthermore, the method exhibits stable behavior in the distributional tails, where classical inversion techniques characteristically deteriorate. We illustrate the practical utility of our results through applications to simultaneous confidence regions and multivariate reliability models. The proposed framework extends naturally to related distributions in the gamma family, offering a flexible and efficient computational tool for high-dimensional statistical inference.

**Keywords:** multivariate gamma distribution, numerical integration, characteristic function inversion, quadratic forms, computational statistics

# Abstract

## Complex-Function Integral Representations for Multivariate Gamma Distributions over the Cube $(-\pi, \pi]^p$

This paper develops and analyzes three distinct complex-function integral representations for the density and distribution functions of multivariate gamma distributions, formulated as integrals over the $p$-dimensional cube $(-\pi, \pi]^p$. Multivariate gamma distributions arise naturally in reliability theory, multivariate hydrology, and the statistical analysis of positively correlated non-negative random vectors, yet their practical utility has long been hampered by the analytical intractability and computational cost of their densities, which are traditionally expressed through infinite series of zonal polynomials or hypergeometric functions of matrix argument.

We propose a unified framework in which the joint density is recovered by integrating a suitable complex-valued kernel—derived from the characteristic function—over the bounded fundamental domain $(-\pi, \pi]^p$. Within this framework, we distinguish **three representation types**: (i) a *direct inversion representation*, which expresses the density as the real part of a Fourier-type integral of the characteristic function; (ii) a *logarithmic-derivative representation*, which reformulates the integrand through the analytic continuation of the cumulant generating function to reduce oscillation near the origin; and (iii) a *saddlepoint-adjusted representation*, which combines a complex deformation of the integration contour with the bounded cubic domain to concentrate mass near the dominant singularity. For each type, we establish existence, uniqueness, and the analytic conditions under which the representation is valid, and we characterize the smoothness and periodicity of the integrand that make the cube the natural domain of integration.

The principal contribution lies in the **numerical advantages** of these bounded-domain formulations relative to classical series expansions and infinite-domain inversion formulas. Because the integration domain is compact and the integrands are periodic, tensor-product quadrature and trapezoidal rules achieve *spectral (super-algebraic) convergence*, avoiding the truncation errors and slow convergence of zonal-polynomial series in high correlation regimes. We demonstrate that the representations remain numerically stable across a broad range of shape and correlation parameters, scale gracefully with dimension $p$ through sparse-grid and randomized quadrature schemes, and permit straightforward computation of marginal, conditional, and tail probabilities. Comparative experiments against existing methods confirm substantial reductions in computational effort at prescribed accuracy, with the saddlepoint-adjusted representation proving especially effective for far-tail evaluation.

These results provide a practical and theoretically grounded toolkit for the exact numerical treatment of multivariate gamma models, and the underlying cubic-domain methodology extends readily to other infinitely divisible multivariate distributions.
